reason:
Attacked and it holds, including the page correction the verifier made. I pulled the raw wikitext of the scan-backed page en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_Jade_Mountain.djvu/152 and it prints, under the centred heading 'Mêng Hao-jan' with the Chinese characters, two poems: A NIGHT-MOORING ON THE CHIEN-TE RIVER first, then A SPRING MORNING, exactly as the evidence says. The four lines are character for character what the card proposes, including the unspaced em dash after 'birds' and the four line heads I, Everywhere, But, And: 'I awake light-hearted this morning of spring, / Everywhere round me the singing of birds— / But now I remember the night, the storm, / And I wonder how many blossoms were broken.' The page's own running-folio template at the foot renders 108, so the printed page is 108 and 152 is the djvu sequence; the verifier's correction is right and the old 152 would have been a false page.
Attribution checked independently of the scan: the Wikisource mainspace header for The Jade Mountain/A Spring Morning carries section_author = Meng Haoran, section = A Spring Morning, translator1 = Witter Bynner, translator2 = Jiang Kanghu. Meng Haoran is not banned and stands at 0 of 3 under both Meng Haoran and Meng Hao-jan; shipped.js returns no hit and no near hit. The Jade Mountain is 1929, in scope, and Poetry is the form of the work. Source line is 85 characters, leads with the name, carries no dash, and puts the translation in parentheses last. Verse keeps its line breaks in the edition's lineation, the quotation ends in a full stop, and there is no straight double quote anywhere. On theme it is a spring-morning poem for a month called Renewal and the Way, and it is publishable.
One optional tightening, not a refutation. The title page reads 'Translated by Witter Bynner from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu', and Wikisource lists Jiang Kanghu as a second translator. Naming Bynner alone is the standard citation and the evidence block already records the fuller form, so the source line is fine as it stands; I flag it only so nobody is surprised later. The note is accurate: the 1929 edition does print the poet as Mêng Hao-jan, and the card's modern Meng Haoran is the right byline with the note carrying the old spelling.
